title: DOAH 26-0051 Recommended Order: RONNIE ROBERTS vs. MIAMI INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
RONNIE ROBERTS,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0051
MIAMI INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
Pursuant to notice, a final hearing in this case was conducted before
Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Mary Li Creasy of the Division of
Administrative Hearings (“DOAH”) by Zoom conference on April 8, 2026.
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Ronnie L. Roberts, pro se
1287 Hopewell Road
Morganton, North Carolina 28655
For Respondent: Narinah P. Jean-Baptiste, Esquire
Miami-Dade County Attorney’s Office
111 Northwest 1st Street, Suite 2810
Miami, Florida 33134
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether Petitioner was unlawfully discriminated against by denial of
assistive services (wheelchair access and disability seating) at the Miami
airport in violation of the Florida Civil Rights Act (“FCRA”); and, if so, what
is the appropriate remedy.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On June 10, 2025, Petitioner, Ronnie Roberts, filed a Charge of
Discrimination with the Florida Commission on Human Relations (“FCHR”),
alleging that Respondent, Miami International Airport (“MIA” or
“Respondent”), unlawfully discriminated against him in a place of public
accommodation by failing to provide him a wheelchair or appropriate seating
while he waited eight hours for a flight on Delta Airlines (“Delta”).
On December 5, 2025, FCHR issued a Notice of Determination to
Petitioner, indicating that FCHR found “no reasonable cause” to believe that
discrimination occurred. Petitioner elected to contest the decision and pursue
administrative remedies by filing a Petition for Relief (“Petition”) with FCHR.
FCHR transmitted the Petition to DOAH on January 6, 2026, and the
undersigned was assigned to hear the case.
The final hearing was held as scheduled on April 8, 2026. At the hearing,
Petitioner testified on his own behalf. He also presented the testimony of
three witnesses: Karen Britton, Petitioner’s wife; Danielle Bishop,
Petitioner’s daughter; and Secolia Bishop, Petitioner’s daughter. Petitioner’s
Exhibits 1 through 34 were admitted.1 Respondent presented the testimony
of Natalie Pavlik, Former Americans with Disabilities Act (“ADA”)
Coordinator for MIA. Respondent’s Exhibits 1 through 7 were admitted into
evidence.
The deadline for submission of proposed recommended orders by the
parties was set for May 15, 2026. Petitioner submitted a letter summarizing
his argument, and MIA timely submitted a Proposed Recommended Order,
both of which were given consideration in the preparation of this
1 Respondent agreed to admit all of Petitioner’s Exhibits 1 through 34. However, Petitioner
did not submit Exhibits 15 and 31 onto the docket, and, therefore, they were not considered.
2

Recommended Order. Except as otherwise indicated, citations to Florida
Statutes refer to the 2024 version in effect at the time of the alleged violation.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The Parties
1. MIA2 is a Department of Miami-Dade County, Florida, which is a
political subdivision of the State of Florida charged with operating a local
government within the geographic boundaries of Miami-Dade County,
Florida.
2. Petitioner, Ronnie Roberts, is a 61-year-old individual who has multiple
documented physical disabilities, including a neurological seizure disorder,
and history of multiple knee, back, and leg surgeries, which limit his
mobility. He regularly uses a walker and/or cane for ambulation.
The September 20, 2024, Incident
3. On September 20, 2024, Petitioner arrived at MIA at approximately
10:00 a.m. with his wife, Karen Britton, his stepdaughters, Danielle Bishop
and Secolia Bishop, and his four-year-old granddaughter. The family had
returned from a birthday cruise and was departing on a Delta flight to
Raleigh-Durham, North Carolina, scheduled for approximately 6:30 p.m. that
evening.
4. Petitioner did not bring his walker or cane to the airport. However,
Petitioner’s disability was visibly apparent through his physical condition,
use of mobility aids, and disability indicators, including the use of a
sunflower lanyard.3
2 Respondent refers to itself in its Proposed Recommended Order as Miami-Dade County
Aviation Department. This is inconsistent with how Respondent was identified throughout
the FCHR process and the style of the case. Accordingly, the undersigned is referring to
Respondent as MIA.
3 A sunflower lanyard is a globally recognized symbol used to discreetly indicate that the
wearer has a hidden, non-visible disability. It alerts staff and the public that the wearer may
need extra time, assistance, or simply more understanding. They are provided free at the
information desk in many major airports or may be purchased online.
3

5. Upon arriving at the airport, Petitioner and his family asked various
individuals within the terminal about wheelchair assistance. The individuals
they approached consistently directed them to Delta as the party responsible
for providing wheelchair services.
6. Petitioner and his family eventually located the Delta ticket counter
area. A Delta employee informed the family that wheelchair assistance was
available, but pursuant to Delta’s policy, wheelchair service would escort
Petitioner directly to his gate.
7. Petitioner did not accept the offer of wheelchair escort to his gate.
Instead, Petitioner and his family left for a little while and then decided to
return to the Delta counter to ask if the airport or Delta could loan them a
wheelchair for use around the airport.
8. The Delta agent explained that they could not provide Petitioner with a
wheelchair eight hours before his flight to roam about the airport due to
liability issues and that the airport does not offer wheelchair services.
9. The Delta agent offered Petitioner and his family the seating that was
available near doors 22 and 23, which was across from the Delta ticket
counters. According to Petitioner and his family, multiple cruise ship
passengers arrived at or near the same time and seating in the terminal was
extremely limited with some passengers sitting on the floor.
10. Petitioner’s daughters approached multiple individuals throughout the
terminal regarding wheelchair access. Each individual directed them to the
airline as the responsible party.
11. MIA maintains multiple passenger accessibility reporting channels
throughout its terminals, including posted screens with ADA Coordinator
contact information, QR codes for direct complaint submission, and staffed
information counters. Neither Petitioner nor his family members contacted
MIA’s ADA Coordinator, approached any MIA customer service or
information counter, or utilized any of the MIA accessibility contact resources
posted throughout the terminal on the date of the incident.
4

12. Approximately 35 to 40 minutes after arriving at the airport, when
attempting to use the restroom, Petitioner collapsed on the airport floor, lost
consciousness for about 15 minutes, and was transported by ambulance to
Jackson West Hospital. After being seen and treated in the Emergency Room,
Petitioner returned to the airport. Upon his return, individuals, whom he
assumed were airport employees, provided him wheelchair assistance when
he entered the terminal.
Post-Incident Investigation by MIA
13. Initially, Petitioner characterized the fall as the result of a wet and
slippery substance on the floor. Petitioner’s wife, Ms. Britton, acting on his
behalf, reported to airport personnel that Petitioner had slipped and fallen in
a wet area at MIA. After reaching out to Risk Management and being
redirected to the janitorial company who told Petitioner that they would not
be covering him under their insurance, Petitioner then changed his narrative
and filed a complaint of discrimination based on unlawful public
accommodation practices.4
14. Natalie Pavlik, MIA’s then ADA Coordinator, and current Special
Projects Administrator, investigated Petitioner’s complaint and testified that
MIA’s sole responsibility is to ensure the physical accessibility of its terminal
facilities. Wheelchair assistance to individual passengers is the responsibility
of the air carrier under the Air Carrier Access Act (“ACAA”). MIA does not
employ, supervise, or deploy wheelchair personnel at the airport. Those
individuals are employed by or contracted through the airlines. MIA has not
contractually agreed to provide wheelchair services to any airline’s
passengers.
15. MIA provides accessible seating both at pre-security and post-security
areas of the airport, including near doors 22 and 23 adjacent to the Delta
ticket counters, with additional general seating available immediately
4 Petitioner’s credibility and that of his witnesses was somewhat lessened by this
contradictory explanation of what occurred and why he was injured.
5

adjacent to the designated accessible area. This seating was available and
operational on the date of the incident.
16. Contrary to Petitioner’s allegation that there were no readily available
seats throughout the entire airport, MIA received no complaints, service
requests, or escalations from Petitioner, his family, or any other airport
passengers on the date of the incident. The only MIA record from that date
pertaining to Petitioner is a fire and rescue incident report filed after his fall.
17. Ms. Pavlik reviewed Petitioner’s Exhibit 5, video footage from inside
the terminal where an individual speaks with Petitioner’s daughter, and
testified that the individual depicted is not an MIA employee. Based on the
uniform and logo visible in the footage, the individual is consistent with a
Maximus Global Services employee, a wheelchair contractor employed by
Delta, not MIA.
18. Ms. Pavlik also reviewed Petitioner’s Exhibit 8, video footage from
inside the terminal where an individual directs Petitioner and his family to
the airline for assistance, and testified that the individual depicted wears a
green badge. MIA employees wear blue badges exclusively. A green badge
identifies a contractor, not an MIA employee.
19. Petitioner’s stepdaughter, Ms. Bishop, testified that she assumed
the individuals she encountered were airport employees because they wore
badges. No individual identified themselves as an MIA employee, and
Ms. Bishop could not confirm the employer of any individual beyond the
Delta ticket counter employee. No evidence was presented that demonstrated
Petitioner or his family made any contact with an MIA employee to seek
wheelchair or seating assistance on the date of the incident.
20. Ms. Pavlik explained that if Petitioner or his family had notified an
MIA employee of the need for additional seating, temporary seating could
have been made available immediately.
6

21. The Federal Aviation Administration conducted a compliance audit of
MIA in December 2024, with no findings of non-compliance related to
accessibility programs, services, or physical infrastructure.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
22. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter of this
cause pursuant to sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11(7), Florida Statutes
(2025).
23. Petitioner alleges that MIA unlawfully discriminated against him on
the basis of disability by failing to provide him a wheelchair and proper
seating. Petitioner contends that, but for Respondent’s failure to provide him
wheelchair or seating, he would not have fallen and suffered injuries,
including worsening pain, increased seizure activity, reduced mobility,
emotional distress, diminished quality of life, and continuing physical
impairment.
Burden of Proof
24. Petitioner has the burden of proving that Respondent failed to provide
full and equal enjoyment of its accommodations on the basis of his handicap.
Fla. Dep’t of Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981).
Petitioner must prove the elements of public accommodation discrimination
by a preponderance of the evidence. § 120.57(1)(j), Fla. Stat.; see Young v.
Dep’t of Cmty. Aff., 625 So. 2d 831 (Fla. 1993).
Public Accommodation Discrimination
25. The FCRA is codified at sections 760.01 through 760.11. Section
760.08, titled “Discrimination in places of public accommodation,” states:
“[a]ll persons are entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the goods,
services, facilities, privileges, advantages, and accommodations of any place
of public accommodation without discrimination or segregation on the ground
of race, color, national origin, sex, pregnancy, handicap, familial status, or
7

religion.” This provision prohibits discrimination against protected classes,
including handicapped persons, in places of public accommodation.
26. The FCRA defines the term “public accommodations” as “places of
public accommodation, lodgings, facilities principally engaged in selling food
for consumption on the premises, gasoline stations, places of exhibition or
entertainment, and other covered establishments.” § 760.02(11), Fla. Stat.
The statute specifically enumerates certain establishments that qualify as
places of public accommodation, including “any motion picture theater,
theater, concert hall, sports arena, stadium, or other place of exhibition or
entertainment.” Id. Notably, the statutory definition does not expressly
include airports, transportation facilities, or common carriers within the
enumerated categories of public accommodations under the FCRA.
27. Florida courts apply the doctrine of expressio unius est exclusio alterius
when interpreting the FCRA’s definition of public accommodations, meaning
that the Legislature’s inclusion of specific establishments implies the
exclusion of others not listed. Okposio v. Barry Univ., 252 So. 3d 1290, 1292
(Fla. 1st DCA 2018). In Okposio, the court held that despite a university
having libraries or “places of entertainment” on its premises, it was not a
place of public accommodation under the FCRA. Id. at 1291. The court
reasoned that “had the Florida Legislature wished to include such places
within its definition of ‘public accommodations,’ it certainly could have done
so.” Id. at 1292.
28. Airports, which are also not enumerated in section 760.02(11), would
similarly fall outside the FCRA’s definition of public accommodations.
29. Because the FCRA is substantially similar to the ADA, courts construe
the two in conformity. Abadi v. Walt Disney World Parks & Resorts, 338 So.
3d 1101, 1104 (Fla. 1st DCA 2022).
30. To prevail on an ADA public accommodation claim in Florida, a
Petitioner must prove: (1) that Petitioner is disabled within the meaning of
the ADA; (2) that Respondent owns, leases, or operates a place of public
8

accommodation; and (3) that Respondent discriminated against the Petitioner
within the meaning of the ADA. Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort
Condo. Owners Ass’n, Inc., 2026 WL 824959, at *3 (S.D. Ala. Mar. 25, 2026).
See also Kennedy v. Floridian Hotel, Inc., 998 F.3d 1221, 1231 (11th Cir.
2021) (applying the same factors).
31. Petitioner meets the first prong. His disabilities are documented and
not in dispute. However, his claim fails on the second prong. As explained in
more detail below, MIA does not own, lease, or operate a place of public
accommodation within the meaning of the ADA or the FCRA. Accordingly,
the third prong need not be reached. Even assuming that Petitioner
demonstrated the applicability of the ADA and the FCRA, he does not meet
the third prong because he failed to put forth evidence that any
representative of MIA discriminated against him.
Title II of the ADA Applies to Governmental Entities–Not Title III
32. The ADA is divided into separate titles that govern distinct categories
of entities with distinct legal obligations. “Title I prohibits discrimination in
private employment; Title II prohibits discrimination by public entities; and
Title III prohibits discrimination by a ‘place of public accommodation,’ which
is a private entity that offers commercial services to the public.” A.L. by &
through D.L. v. Walt Disney Parks & Resorts US, Inc., 900 F.3d 1270, 1289
(11th Cir. 2018). This structural distinction is dispositive of Petitioner’s
claim.
33. Title II of the ADA applies to public entities, state and local
governments and their agencies and instrumentalities. 42 U.S.C. § 12132.
MIA, as a department of Miami-Dade County, is a public entity subject to
Title II of the ADA, not Title III.
34. Title III of the ADA applies to places of public accommodation
operated by private entities. 42 U.S.C. § 12182(a). Title III expressly excludes
facilities covered by Title II from its public accommodation provisions.
42 U.S.C. § 12181. Because MIA is a governmental airport operator subject to
9

Title II, Title III does not apply, and Petitioner cannot maintain a Title III
public accommodation claim against MIA.
35. Title II obligations attach to the services and programs the public
entity itself controls and operates. 42 U.S.C. § 12132. Specifically, in this
case, the ACAA has expressly assigned responsibility for wheelchair service
to Delta. Therefore, a Title II claim against MIA for that same service cannot
stand. The wheelchair assistance Petitioner sought is a service the law
assigns to the airlines, not to MIA. See 14 C.F.R. § 382.91.
36. Even if MIA were a private entity potentially covered by Title III,
airport terminals are not included within the enumerated categories of places
of public accommodation under Title III. 42 U.S.C. § 12181(7). Title III of the
ADA prohibits discrimination in public accommodations, commercial
facilities, and specified public transportation. 42 U.S.C. § 12181. Under this
framework, a “public accommodation” includes “a terminal, depot, or other
station used for specified public transportation.” See 42 U.S.C. § 12181(7)(G).
The statute defines “specified public transportation” as “transportation by
bus, rail, or any other conveyance (other than by aircraft) that provides the
general public with general or special service (including charter service) on a
regular and continuing basis.” 42 U.S.C. § 12181(10). Reading these
provisions together, the statutory language is unambiguous and clearly
establishes that airplanes and terminals used for air travel are excluded from
coverage under Title III of the ADA. Mennella v. Am. Airlines, Inc., No. 17-cv-
21915-GAYLES, 2017 WL 6560467, at *2 (S.D. Fla. Dec. 22, 2017). See also
Lopez v. Jet Blue Airways, 662 F.3d 593, 599 (2nd Cir. 2011)( Public
transportation terminals, depots, or stations used primarily to facilitate air
transportation are not “public accommodation[s]” for purposes of Title III of
the ADA.).
37. Accordingly, even under Title III of the ADA, no cognizable public
accommodation claim lies against MIA as the governmental operator of MIA.
10

Air Carrier Access Act
38. The ACAA establishes the comprehensive federal framework
governing disability accommodations in air travel. Under the ACAA, the
obligation to provide wheelchair and mobility assistance to passengers rests
explicitly and exclusively with the air carrier—not the airport operator. 14
C.F.R. § 382.91(a). The air carrier is required to provide wheelchair
assistance to passengers who request it, including assistance through the
terminal, to and from the gate, and during boarding and deplaning. 14 C.F.R.
§ 382.91(b).
39. Title 49 C.F.R. § 27.71 provides that “airport operators shall ensure
that the terminal facilities and services subject to this section shall be readily
accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities, including individuals
who use wheelchairs.” 49 C.F.R. § 27.71(b). Airport operators are in
compliance with this statute if they meet requirements applying to state and
local government programs or activities and facilities under Department of
Justice (DOJ) regulations implementing Title II of the ADA. Id.
40. An air carrier and airport operator may contract to delegate these
responsibilities. 49 C.F.R. § 27.71(f). Contracts or leases between carriers and
airport operators concerning the use of airport facilities must set forth the
respective responsibilities of the parties for the provision of accessible
facilities and services to individuals with disabilities for carriers. Id. Simply
put, airports receiving federal financial assistance have specific
responsibilities to ensure accessibility for individuals with disabilities,
including maintaining accessible paths between gates and aircraft boarding
areas, establishing clear contractual responsibilities with carriers, and
submitting transition plans for existing facilities.
41. Here, MIA has not contractually assumed any obligation to provide
wheelchair services to any airline’s passengers. Ms. Pavlik testified without
contradiction that MIA does not employ, supervise, or deploy the personnel
who provide wheelchair assistance to passengers at the airport. Those
11

individuals are employed by or contracted through the airlines—in this case,
Delta, through its contractor, MGS. An airport operator may assume
additional responsibilities through contract, but no such contract exists here.
42. The accommodation Petitioner sought, wheelchair assistance and
seating, was offered by Delta through its contractor, MGS, consistent with
the airline’s obligations under the ACAA. That offer included a direct escort
to Petitioner’s gate and seating near the ticket counter. Petitioner declined
the offer. A party who is offered the precise accommodation the law requires
and declines that offer cannot subsequently maintain that the
accommodation was denied. Bryant v. Caritas Norwood Hosp., 345 F. Supp.
2d 155, 168 (D. Mass. 2004).
Conclusion
43. Although Petitioner undoubtedly sustained significant injuries at
MIA, he failed to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that he
was entitled to, and was denied, reasonable accommodations from MIA, or
that he is entitled to any damages recoverable against this Respondent
pursuant to the FCRA.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order finding that Petitioner, Ronnie Roberts, did not prove that
Respondent, Miami International Airport, committed an unlawful public
accommodation practice against him, and dismissing his Petition for Relief
from an unlawful public accommodation practice.
12

Hillsborough County, Florida.
